extracted.intended_audience: students, readers, and practitioners of poetry and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and judging poetry—principles of good criticism and poetic practice drawn from Pope's Essay on Criticism and its notes. Emphasizes critic virtues, stylistic balance, and learning from classical models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrain censure; prefer silence to spite
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Tis best sometimes your censure to restrain, And charitably let the dull be vain; Your silence there is better than your spite
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attack every poor writer — silence can be more charitable and effective than spiteful criticism. Continued railing only gives bad writers more opportunity ('For who can rail so long as they can write?') and false attacks may revive their efforts rather than correct them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'bookful blockhead' — don't be ignorant pedantry
rubrics_metrics.description: The bookful blockhead ignorantly read, With loads of learned lumber in his head, With his own tongue still edifies his ears, And always listening to himself appears
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics must not merely parade learning or heap up quotations; avoid being someone who reads without understanding and who habitually assaults books. Self‑important, rote learnedness that lacks judgment is a vice in criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be unbiased and free from prepossession
rubrics_metrics.description: Still pleased to teach, and yet not proud to know? Unbiased, or by favor, or in spite, Not dully prepossess'd, nor blindly right;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgments should not be warped by personal favor or spite; a critic should teach without pride and avoid fixed preconceptions that prevent fair assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modestly bold and humanly severe; honest in correction and praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Though learned, well-bred, and though well bred, sincere, Modestly bold, and humanly severe, Who to a friend his faults can freely show, And gladly praise the merit of a foe?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good critic is both courageous and humane: willing to point out friends' faults, to praise enemies when deserved, and to temper severity with modesty and sincerity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possess an exact yet unconfined taste and knowledge of books and mankind
rubrics_metrics.description: Blessed with a taste exact, yet unconfined; A knowledge both of books and human kind; Generous converse, a soul exempt from pride; And love to praise, with reason on his side?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine precise discernment with openness; have learning in literature and understanding of human nature; be generous, humble, and ready to praise when reason warrants it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance passion in writing with coolness in judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: He who supreme in judgment as in wit, ... Yet judged with coolness though he sung with fire; Our critics take a contrary extreme — They judge with fury, but they write with phlegm:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modelled on Horace: write with vigor and passion but judge calmly and fairly. Avoid the mismatch of furious judgment paired with dull, lifeless writing (or vice versa).

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from classical authorities and exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: The Stagirite first left the shore... Horace still charms with graceful negligence... In grave Quintilian's copious work we find... Thee bold Longinus! all the Nine inspire
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study and adopt lessons from classical critics (Aristotle, Horace, Quintilian, Longinus, etc.); let exemplary works and critics inform both rules and practice—examples should reinforce precepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style: aim for graceful negligence and natural method
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace still charms with graceful negligence, And without method talks us into sense; Will like a friend familiarly convey The truest notions in the easiest way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for an artful ease in expression: method should not be ostentatious; good style often appears natural and familiar while conveying truth clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat rules as practical tools 'to arm the hand'
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus useful arms in magazines we place, All ranged in order, and dispos'd with grace, But less to please the eye, than arm the hand, Still fit for use, and ready at command.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical rules are instruments meant to be applied in practice, not mere ornament or display; rules should serve to guide writing and revision practically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid forced, exhausted, or overstrained writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Strain out the last dull droppings of their sense, And rhyme with all the rage of impotence!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets should not squeeze out tired or strained lines — avoid overwrought rhymes and exhausted conceits; when the muse is spent, refrain rather than producing feeble verse.
